steps.description:
Create a program that performs the following: 1. Ask the user to input an integer. 2. Divide it by 2 using floor division (//) and display the result (whole number of the division). 3. Repeat step (2) until the integer is 0.

Follow the test output display format.

Test Input

15

10

2

Test Output (Red Text - User Input) Test your program with the examples below:

Example 1 Input number: 15 7 3 1 0

Example 2 Input number: 10 5 2 1 0

Example 3 Input number: 2 1 0

Create a program that performs the following: 1. Ask the user to input an integer. 2. Using floor division (//) and modulus (%), display the quotient (whole number) and remainder when the integer is divided by 2. 3. Set the integer to the quotient. 4. Repeat steps (2) to (3) until the integer is 0.

Follow the test output display format.

Hint: - floor division operator "//" returns the whole number, eg. 7 // 2 = 3 - modulus operator "%" returns the remainder, eg. 7 % 2 = 1

Test Input

15

10

2

Test Output (Red Text - User Input) Test your program with the examples below:

Example 1 Input number: 15 15/2 Quotient 7 Remainder 1 7/2 Quotient 3 Remainder 1 3/2 Quotient 1 Remainder 1 1/2 Quotient 0 Remainder 1

Example 2 Input number: 10 10/2 Quotient 5 Remainder 0 5/2 Quotient 2 Remainder 1 2/2 Quotient 1 Remainder 0 1/2 Quotient 0 Remainder 1

Example 3 Input number: 2 2/2 Quotient 1 Remainder 0 1/2 Quotient 0 Remainder 1

A number can be converted to its binary representation by using division by 2. Below shows an example with integer number 12:

12/2 gives 6 with remainder 0 (note that this is the last bit) 6/2 gives 3 with remainder 0 3/2 gives 1 with remainder 1 1/2 gives 0 with remainder 1 (note that this is the first bit)

The binary is formed by the remainders from bottom-up: 1100

Write a program that asks the user to enter a positive number and convert it to a binary. Write your own algorithm and do not use python's built-in bin() function.

Test Input 3

12

44

Test Output (Red Text - User Input) Test your program with the examples below:

Example 1 Input number: 3 1 1

Example 2 Input number: 12 1 1 0 0

Example 3 Input number: 44 1 0 1 1 0 0

A binary can be converted to its decimal value by using the formular bit x (2 to the power of bit-position). Position 0 starts from the right most bit. Below shows an example using binary number 1100:

Bit position: 3 2 1 0 Binary: 1 1 0 0 1 x 2**3 = 8 1 x 2**2 = 4 0 x 2**1 = 0 0 x 2**0 = 0

The number for 1100 is equal to 8+4+0+0 = 12

Write a program ask the user to enter a binary number and convert to its decimal value.

Follow the test output display format.

Note: a number can be stored in a larger number of bits. For example, 3 is represented by the 2-bit binary 11. It can also be represented with more bits such as 011, 0011, 00011, etc.

Test Input 01

001

1111

011010

Test Output (Red Text - User Input) Test your program with the examples below:

Example 1 Input binary: 01 1

Example 2 Input binary: 001 1

Example 3 Input binary: 1111 15

Example 4 Input binary: 011010 26
